### Skill: artifact-design
Path: bundled:artifact-design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# kconfig-tweak

Command-line tool for modifying `.config` files without launching interactive menuconfig.

## Quick Reference

```bash
# Enable/disable options
kconfig-tweak --enable DEBUG_INFO
kconfig-tweak --disable MODULES
kconfig-tweak -e SMP -d PREEMPT    # Multiple in one command

# Set values
kconfig-tweak --set-val LOG_BUF_SHIFT 17
kconfig-tweak --set-str LOCALVERSION "-custom"

# Query state
kconfig-tweak --state DEBUG_INFO   # Returns: y, n, m, or undef

# Specify config file
kconfig-tweak --file boards/myboard/.config --enable USB

# Module support
kconfig-tweak --module DRM         # Set to m (module)
```

## Commands

| Command | Short | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--enable OPTION` | `-e` | Set option to y |
| `--disable OPTION` | `-d` | Set option to n |
| `--module OPTION` | `-m` | Set option to m (module) |
| `--set-val OPTION VALUE` | - | Set integer/hex value |
| `--set-str OPTION STRING` | - | Set string value (quoted) |
| `--undefine OPTION` | `-u` | Remove option definition |
| `--state OPTION` | `-s` | Query current state |

## Position Control

Insert options after a specific option (useful for maintaining config order):

```bash
kconfig-tweak --enable-after USB USB_STORAGE    # -E
kconfig-tweak --disable-after NET BRIDGE        # -D
kconfig-tweak --module-after DRM DRM_I915       # -M
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--file FILE` | Target config file (default: .config) |
| `--keep-case` / `-k` | Preserve symbol case (default: auto-uppercase) |

## Environment Variables

- `CONFIG_` - Symbol prefix (default: "CONFIG_")

## Common Patterns

### Batch Configuration
```bash
# Enable multiple debug options
kconfig-tweak -e DEBUG_INFO -e DEBUG_FS -e KALLSYMS

# Configure network stack
kconfig-tweak --file .config \
  -e NET -e INET -e IPV6 \
  --set-val TCP_CONG_CUBIC y
```

### CI/CD Integration
```bash
# Start from defconfig, then customize
make defconfig
kconfig-tweak -e DEBUG_INFO -d MODULES
make olddefconfig  # Resolve dependencies
```

### Query Before Modify
```bash
# Check current state
STATE=$(kconfig-tweak -s PREEMPT)
if [ "$STATE" = "y" ]; then
  kconfig-tweak -d PREEMPT
fi
```

## Notes

- kconfig-tweak does NOT validate dependencies; run `make olddefconfig` after modifications
- Symbol names auto-uppercase unless `--keep-case` is used
- Changes are immediate; no confirmation prompt

30	  @font-face { font-family: "Acme Sans"; src: url(AcmeSans.woff2) }
31	</style>
32	```
33	
34	The build checks that the file is really a font. It adds the font to the list of files to upload as assets, along with the images. After the deck is saved, the font's `src` is the asset url the upload or copy returned (`_blob/<id>`, with or without a leading `/`), or the `project/ds/…` path it was installed on. Leave it exactly as it is when you edit a saved deck.
35	
36	Never write a font as a `data:` URI. If the file cannot be uploaded, do not declare that face: use a Google Fonts or basic face instead, and tell the user. (With `scripts/make.ts`, use `--inline-images`.)
37	
38	A static font file with only one weight will render every weight at that one weight. Prefer a variable font file, or the single weight you use the most. The `<style>` section may hold nothing but `@font-face` rules.
39	
40	Symbols that the typeface does not include (for example ✓ ✗ ★ ☐ and most dingbats) fall back to a system font. For a check mark, write `<x-icon name="Check">`. For a "no", use a word or a plain −.
41	
42	## Default picks — prefer these unless the brief says otherwise
43	
44	All of these are Google Fonts families. Load the ones you choose with one `<link>`, each as `family=Name+With+Spaces` plus a `:wght@` range covering the weights you use, names exactly as shown here.
45	
46	**Text (body) typeface — choose ONE. If your deck uses only one typeface, it will be this one.**
47	
48	- sans: `DM Sans` (modern consumer) · `Nunito Sans` (friendly neutral) · `Rubik` (soft-cornered grotesk, product) · `IBM Plex Sans` (technical, enterprise) · `Public Sans` (civic, quiet)
49	- rounded: `Nunito` (education, wellness) · `Quicksand` (light, airy) · `Fredoka` (kids, bold consumer)
50	- serif: `EB Garamond` (academic, heritage) · `Libre Baskerville` (editorial, reports)
51	- slab: `Domine` (friendly-serious)
52	- mono: `JetBrains Mono` · `Fira Code` (developer decks, code)
53	
54	**Display (heading) typeface — choose ONE from a different row than your text typeface.**
55	
56	- sans: `DM Sans` · `Rubik`
57	- serif: `EB Garamond` · `Libre Baskerville` · `Cormorant Garamond` (delicate; use only at display sizes)
58	- slab: `Domine`
59	- condensed: `Oswald` (posters, sports, statements)
60	- rounded: `Nunito` · `Fredoka`
61	- calligraphic: `Dancing Script` (use for only one line, never for body text)
62	- hand-drawn: `Caveat` (use for one accent line, never for body text)
63	
64	You can also use any other typeface on Google Fonts, like Playfair Display, Lora, Bitter, Work Sans, Space Grotesk, Montserrat, Syne, and others. This is fine when you have a deliberate design direction.
65	
66	## Pairings by mood (headings + text)
67	
68	- Editorial / magazine: `Rubik` + `Libre Baskerville`, or just `Libre Baskerville` (headings at 700)
69	- Luxury / hospitality: `Cormorant Garamond` + `Rubik` (light)
70	- Institutional / research / policy: `EB Garamond` + `IBM Plex Sans`, `Libre Baskerville` + `Public Sans`, or `Source Serif 4` + `IBM Plex Sans`
71	- Literary / non-profit / education: `Domine` + `Nunito Sans`, or just `Libre Baskerville`
72	- Academic / heritage: just `EB Garamond` (headings at 600)
73	- Product / startup / SaaS: just `DM Sans`, or `Rubik` + `Domine`
74	- Developer / infrastructure: `IBM Plex Sans` + `JetBrains Mono`, or `Rubik` + `Fira Code`
75	- Bold / poster / sports: `Oswald` + `Public Sans`, or `Oswald` + `Rubik`
76	- Playful / consumer: `Fredoka` + `Nunito Sans`, just `Quicksand`, or a `Caveat` accent line over `Nunito Sans`
77	- Quiet / minimal: just `Public Sans`
78	- Celebratory / invitation: `Dancing Script` (one line) + `EB Garamond`
79	
80	Vary between decks. Do not always reach for the same pairing. Do not choose a typeface only because it is first in a list.
81	
82	## Rules that keep a deck from looking generic
83	
84	The checklist in SKILL.md is the rule set. Here are the numbers behind it:
85	
86	- **Two faces is the norm; a third only when it has a clear job.** One of them is the display face. A distinctive display face with a refined text face looks better than two safe faces.
87	- **Color in hex, chosen once.** Choose one dark color and one light color. You may also choose zero, one, or two accent colors. If you use two accents, they should share the same chroma and lightness but have different hues. Tone the whites and blacks toward the palette. For example, use `#FBFBF8` instead of pure white and `#14213D` instead of pure black. Never use raw `#FFFFFF` or `#000000` unless you want a stark look on purpose. Use two background tones per deck, plus the one accent statement slide. Add a `background` style to every section.
88	- **Contrast is a number.** Body text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. At display sizes, the ratio must be at least 3:1. If you use a light accent color (like `#E8C547`), put dark text on it.
89	- **Color never says it alone.** A status, a good/bad split, the winning bar, a risk level or a highlighted cell also says so in its text ("+4%, over plan"; "High risk"); a dash, a ✓ or an icon standing for a word gets the word beside it (icons, shapes and connectors reach a screen reader as nothing).
90	- **The type scale is the hierarchy.** Use four or five font sizes. For example: 120 / 72 / 44 / 32 / 24. Reuse them across the deck. Use the accent color for eyebrows. Use the dark tone for headings on a light background, or the light tone on a dark background. For body text, use a softened dark color (like `#4A5568` on a light background, or `#BFD8D5` on a dark background).
91	- **Typographic punctuation.** In all the text people read (slides, speaker notes, the deck’s title, section descriptions), type `’` for the apostrophe and the quotation marks of the text’s language (`“ ”` in English, `« »` in French, `„ “` in German). Keep straight `'` and `"` as HTML, CSS and JSON syntax, in code shown on a slide, and for feet and inches.

[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

Its style controls both its background (the "paint") and its layout. - `padding` is the slide margin. 128px is the standard margin. - `display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap` stacks the child elements from top to bottom with space between them. - `justify-content:center` centers the child elements vertically. - `justify-content:flex-end` sinks the child elements to the bottom. A section with no `display` style is a plain column with no gap. There are two ways to place child elements inside a `

Open space appears wherever the flow leaves it. Open space LOW on a slide is correct. Do not reach for `justify-content:center` on every slide. - **Pinned**: Pinned children have `position:absolute`. They leave the flow and sit where their `left`, `right`, `top`, and `bottom` styles say, relative to the section. Give them a `width` (text needs one to wrap), or pin both sides. Use pinned children only for the things flow cannot do: - A source line at the bottom edge - A badge over a corner - A full-bleed photo behind everything, with `position:absolute; left:0; top:0; width:1920px; height:1080px; object-fit:cover`, listed first in the HTML so the other elements paint over it - A magic-move element Put everything else in the flow. [0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:30 · ends 5:25] Meal times can also be set by voice, with no network at all. In a pet's edit screen, one tap starts a three-step dialog: which meal, which hour, then confirm. Each step listens only for its own words. These are the console lines from a real run on the board: two, eight, yes, and meal 2 is set to 08:00 in 9.6 seconds with no false accepts. Two choices keep it safe. We threshold the raw score and never renormalise over the allowed words: renormalising let 86 percent of silence and stray words through the yes-or-no step, while the raw score lets 4.9 percent through. And a word heard twice above 0.25 is accepted, which rescued real dialogs like this hour step. The result goes into the edit dialog, so the owner still taps Save.

VelaPaw · CircuitForge · engineering

52
[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. The panel's chip-select is tied low, so one stray clock edge at the pin handover desynchronised it; a reset after the handover fixed it, and it now runs at 40 MHz with DMA. The rest are on the table: a static-init deadlock, a mic DMA alignment stall, an agent stack in PSRAM, and overlapping USB FIFOs.

[Backup] If asked why this board. We started on Espressif's ESP32-S3-EYE, which has the same chip. The Waveshare 3.5-inch board adds a capacitive touch screen, a PCF85063 real-time clock for meal times, an ES8311 codec with a mic and speaker for voice, a connector for the 5-megapixel OV5640, and 16 MB of flash. [0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

VelaPaw · CircuitForge · engineering

52
[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. The panel's chip-select is tied low, so one stray clock edge at the pin handover desynchronised it; a reset after the handover fixed it, and it now runs at 40 MHz with DMA. The rest are on the table: a static-init deadlock, a mic DMA alignment stall, an agent stack in PSRAM, and overlapping USB FIFOs.

VelaPaw knows who ate." - Aside: `[0:25 · ends 7:20] Where do we stand? Xiaomi's Mijia Smart Pet Feeder 2 Visual Edition, launched this March at 449 yuan crowdfunding and 549 retail, is a polished product: a scale accurate to the gram, a 5-litre hopper, a backup battery and live video. It detects a pet approaching or eating; telling pets apart is not advertised. That is the gap we fill: Mijia knows how much was eaten, VelaPaw knows who ate. (Sources, not to read aloud: news.17173.com, 30 March 2026; global.hk01.com; the mi.com product page for the Xiaomi Smart Pet Food Feeder 2.)` #### roadmap - Title: "From prototype to product". - Chinese line: `从样机到产品：下一步加称重和 Wi-Fi 联网，并把修复回馈 openVela；右图为 AI 生成概念图，尚未制作。` - NEXT STEPS: - Activity: "Hardware · weigh what is actually eaten" / "A load cell under the bowl, not just grams dispensed" - Search: "AI · sharper recognition" / "A pet / no-pet check, then identity tuned to each home" - Globe: "Connectivity · Wi-Fi of its own" / "The agent goes online through a laptop today" - PaperPlane: "openVela · send our fixes upstream" / "USB, audio-buffer and TFLM fixes for ESP32-S3 boards" - "AI-GENERATED CONCEPT · NOT BUILT YET": - `/_blob/5d2ece33e691dd2e7df469ffc1048c54`, alt "AI-generated concept render of a future VelaPaw: a white feeder with a touch screen showing live video, a camera, kibble falling into a steel bowl, and a VelaPaw logo on the base" - `/_blob/169e6327673e4b8776cd3d3e9097bfea`, alt "AI-generated cutaway of the same concept, labelled: touch display, camera, dispense chute, food tank, stainless steel bowl, and a load cell platform under the bowl" - Caption: "Where it leads: a load cell under the bowl". - Strip: "Whatever we add, feeding stays on the board: no cloud, no phone, no account." - Aside: `[0:25 · ends 7:45] Next steps. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. PROJECT DEFENSE · 项目答辩

A timer can't tell two cats apart

2026 首届 openvela AI 硬件开发者大赛

定时喂食器分不清是哪只宠物：抢得快的吃两份，胆小的挨饿，每只都喂一样多，食欲下降也没人发现。

The fastest pet eats it all

A timer drops food at 08:00 for whoever gets there first. The bold cat eats twice; the shy one goes hungry.

Same scoop for every pet

A kitten, a senior on a diet and a cat on prescription food all get the same portion at the same time.

Appetite drops go unseen

Eating less is often the first sign of illness. A feeder that can't tell who ate can't tell who stopped.

结论

VelaPaw feeds the pet, not the clock.

[0:30 · ends 0:45] In homes with several pets, automatic feeders still run on a clock. At eight o'clock food drops for whoever reaches the bowl first, so the bold cat eats twice and the shy one goes hungry. Every pet gets the same scoop. And eating less, often the first sign of illness, goes unnoticed, because the feeder never knows who ate. We wanted a feeder that decides for itself who eats. VelaPaw feeds the pet, not the clock.

[0:30 · ends 1:15] This is the core of VelaPaw. Food drops only when two answers agree. PROJECT DEFENSE · 项目答辩

A working prototype, not a dev board

2026 首届 openvela AI 硬件开发者大赛

完整样机，不是裸开发板：3D 打印外壳和料仓，摄像头装在支架上，步进电机带动拨轮出粮。

The whole feeder, side view

One portion lands in the bowl

[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:30 · ends 5:25] Meal times can also be set by voice, with no network at all. In a pet's edit screen, one tap starts a three-step dialog: which meal, which hour, then confirm. Each step listens only for its own words. These are the console lines from a real run on the board: two, eight, yes, and meal 2 is set to 08:00 in 9.6 seconds with no false accepts. Two choices keep it safe. We threshold the raw score and never renormalise over the allowed words: renormalising let 86 percent of silence and stray words through the yes-or-no step, while the raw score lets 4.9 percent through. The LCD bug alone took about 60 build cycles; a ¥45 logic analyzer finally narrowed it down.

[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. The panel's chip-select is tied low, so one stray clock edge at the pin handover desynchronised it; a reset after the handover fixed it, and it now runs at 40 MHz with DMA. The rest are on the table: a static-init deadlock, a mic DMA alignment stall, an agent stack in PSRAM, and overlapping USB FIFOs.

Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. 61 ms full repaint | | TFLM | Solid blue screen, no crash dump | C++ static-init guard deadlocks on first use | Build with
-fno-threadsafe-statics | The 1.4 MB model runs on the chip | | Audio | Mic capture stalled, seemingly at random | RX DMA hangs when the buffer address is 8 mod 16 | Align audio buffers to 64 bytes | 0 of 193 buffers missed | | Memory | Asking the agent froze the chip | Its stack sat in PSRAM, which goes dark during flash I/O | Move task stacks to internal SRAM | No freezes since | | USB | Agent hung after sending its request | USB TX FIFOs overlapped the RX FIFO in a 256-word RAM | Re-map the FIFOs; fix the OTG + NCM drivers | Back-to-back asks

The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:30 · ends 5:25] Meal times can also be set by voice, with no network at all. In a pet's edit screen, one tap starts a three-step dialog: which meal, which hour, then confirm. Each step listens only for its own words. These are the console lines from a real run on the board: two, eight, yes, and meal 2 is set to 08:00 in 9.6 seconds with no false accepts. Two choices keep it safe. We threshold the raw score and never renormalise over the allowed words: renormalising let 86 percent of silence and stray words through the yes-or-no step, while the raw score lets 4.9 percent through. And a word heard twice above 0.25 is accepted, which rescued real dialogs like this hour step. The result goes into the edit dialog, so the owner still taps Save.

The LCD bug alone took about 60 build cycles; a ¥45 logic analyzer finally narrowed it down.

[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. The panel's chip-select is tied low, so one stray clock edge at the pin handover desynchronised it; a reset after the handover fixed it, and it now runs at 40 MHz with DMA. [0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.

[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. The panel's chip-select is tied low, so one stray clock edge at the pin handover desynchronised it; a reset after the handover fixed it, and it now runs at 40 MHz with DMA. The rest are on the table: a static-init deadlock, a mic DMA alignment stall, an agent stack in PSRAM, and overlapping USB FIFOs.

A stepper rotates CONTINUOUSLY one direction → pockets ratchet inlet→outlet → true per-pocket dosing, and "grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET" becomes literally true. Geared 28BYJ-48 also has strong low-speed torque (resists kibble jams).

49	## Pinout — VERIFIED against the official ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5 schematic netlist (2026-08-02)
50	Native GPIO map:
51	- LCD (ST7796 SPI): IO1 MOSI, **IO3 DC**, **IO4 CS**, IO5 SCLK, IO6 BL. **IO2 is a DEAD PIN** — its net has exactly one node (the SoC). Waveshare never routed the display read-back line, and the LCD connector's SDO (L1.22) is dangling too. This is why the defconfig has `CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=-1`. IO2 is NOT on the header and cannot be used for anything.
52	- I2C bus (touch/RTC/IMU/audio codec/AXP/expander all shared): **IO7 SCL, IO8 SDA**
53	- microSD (SPI): IO9 MISO, IO10 MOSI, IO11 SCLK (SD_CS on expander EXIO3). **Slot is unused → these three are the board's only reusable native GPIOs, and the stepper now owns them.**
54	- I2S audio (ES8311): IO12 MCLK, IO13 SCLK, IO14 ASDOUT, IO15 LRCK, IO16 DSDIN. **PRIVATE BUS — not on any header.** Each net has exactly two nodes: ESP32 + codec. Nothing external can reach them, and nothing external can conflict with them.
55	- Camera (OV5640 DVP): IO17 VSYNC, IO18 HREF, IO21 D7, IO38 XCLK, IO39 D6, IO40 D5, IO41 PCLK, IO42 D4, IO45 D0, IO46 D3, IO47 D1, IO48 D2
56	- USB-C: IO19 (D-), IO20 (D+) — the console (USB-Serial/JTAG) rides here
57	- UART0: IO43 TXD (usable as GPIO), **IO44 RXD — clamped, will NOT drive an output** (the UART mux re-wins over `esp32s3_configgpio`)
58	- IO33–37 dangle (single-node nets); flash + octal PSRAM occupy the IO26–37 region internally
59	- IO0: IMU INT + strapping (avoid)
60	- TCA9554 expander EXIO0–7 (all used): CAM_PWDN, LCD_RST, TP_INT, SD_CS, RTC_INT, AXP_IRQ, SYS_OUT, PA_CTRL.

85	## Onboard audio — free, costs zero GPIOs
86	The -C carries a **microphone** (analog differential into ES8311 `MIC1P`/`MIC1N` via R41/R43) and an **MX1.25 speaker header** driven by an **NS4150B** amp whose enable is `PA_CTRL` = **expander EXIO7**; a **6 Ω 1 W speaker ships in the box**. Codec control (`AU_SCL`/`AU_SDA`) is on the existing IO7/IO8 I²C bus. Because the I²S bus is private (IO12–16), **audio and the stepper cannot physically conflict** — this is the only viable voice-input path, and it needs no new parts and no motor changes. ⚠️ Firmware must not drive 12/13/15/16 as GPIOs once the codec is enabled. NuttX side: `nuttx/drivers/audio/es8311.c` supports `AUDIO_TYPE_INPUT`, and `esp32s3_i2s.c` has `i2s_receive()` with `CONFIG_ESP32S3_I2S0_RX` default y. No ASR engine exists in the tree — keyword spotting would be TFLM, or cloud via `external/bailian_sdk`.

92	## Feeder dispensing — grams -> motion (calibration)
93	The app speaks **grams** (portions ~5-50g, daily limits 20-300g; NOT kg). The dispenser does not measure grams; it is CALIBRATED once:
94	- Measure kibble released per unit of motion: run the auger 1 rotation (or motor 1 s), weigh the output on a kitchen scale -> e.g. `grams_per_rotation` ~= 5g (or `grams_per_second` ~= 8g). Store the constant (NVS/SD so it survives reboot).
95	- **Dispense N grams = run actuator for N / grams_per_unit** (e.g. 20g @ 5g/rot = 4 rotations, or 2.5s @ 8g/s).
96	- This is OPEN-LOOP feeding (no sensor): ~±10-20% accurate, standard for consumer feeders. Fine for v1.

98	**Firmware hook:** `velapaw_feeder_dispense(grams)` (currently mock print) becomes on hardware: `runtime = grams / grams_per_second; drive_servo(GPIO43 LEDC PWM, runtime);`. Nothing above it changes (app stays in grams). Planned backend: hal/feeder_servo.c.

32	## Feeder actuator: 28BYJ-48 stepper (switched from servo 2026-07-18)
33	**Why:** a code review caught a CRITICAL kinematic bug — inlet & outlet are 180° apart, and a servo can only OSCILLATE (zero net rotation), so a pocket filled at the inlet can never reach the outlet: it dispenses the initial charge a few times then **dead-heads forever** ("worst-case demo failure"). Confirmed in firmware (`rotor_index_one` swept 60° and back). A stepper rotates CONTINUOUSLY one direction → pockets ratchet inlet→outlet → true per-pocket dosing, and "grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET" becomes literally true. Geared 28BYJ-48 also has strong low-speed torque (resists kibble jams).

49	## Pinout — VERIFIED against the official ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5 schematic netlist (2026-08-02)
50	Native GPIO map:
51	- LCD (ST7796 SPI): IO1 MOSI, **IO3 DC**, **IO4 CS**, IO5 SCLK, IO6 BL. **IO2 is a DEAD PIN** — its net has exactly one node (the SoC). Waveshare never routed the display read-back line, and the LCD connector's SDO (L1.22) is dangling too. This is why the defconfig has `CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=-1`. IO2 is NOT on the header and cannot be used for anything.
52	- I2C bus (touch/RTC/IMU/audio codec/AXP/expander all shared): **IO7 SCL, IO8 SDA**
53	- microSD (SPI): IO9 MISO, IO10 MOSI, IO11 SCLK (SD_CS on expander EXIO3). **Slot is unused → these three are the board's only reusable native GPIOs, and the stepper now owns them.**
54	- I2S audio (ES8311): IO12 MCLK, IO13 SCLK, IO14 ASDOUT, IO15 LRCK, IO16 DSDIN. **PRIVATE BUS — not on any header.** Each net has exactly two nodes: ESP32 + codec. Nothing external can reach them, and nothing external can conflict with them.
55	- Camera (OV5640 DVP): IO17 VSYNC, IO18 HREF, IO21 D7, IO38 XCLK, IO39 D6, IO40 D5, IO41 PCLK, IO42 D4, IO45 D0, IO46 D3, IO47 D1, IO48 D2
56	- USB-C: IO19 (D-), IO20 (D+) — the console (USB-Serial/JTAG) rides here
57	- UART0: IO43 TXD (usable as GPIO), **IO44 RXD — clamped, will NOT drive an output** (the UART mux re-wins over `esp32s3_configgpio`)
58	- IO33–37 dangle (single-node nets); flash + octal PSRAM occupy the IO26–37 region internally
59	- IO0: IMU INT + strapping (avoid)
60	- TCA9554 expander EXIO0–7 (all used): CAM_PWDN, LCD_RST, TP_INT, SD_CS, RTC_INT, AXP_IRQ, SYS_OUT, PA_CTRL.

85	## Onboard audio — free, costs zero GPIOs
86	The -C carries a **microphone** (analog differential into ES8311 `MIC1P`/`MIC1N` via R41/R43) and an **MX1.25 speaker header** driven by an **NS4150B** amp whose enable is `PA_CTRL` = **expander EXIO7**; a **6 Ω 1 W speaker ships in the box**. Codec control (`AU_SCL`/`AU_SDA`) is on the existing IO7/IO8 I²C bus. Because the I²S bus is private (IO12–16), **audio and the stepper cannot physically conflict** — this is the only viable voice-input path, and it needs no new parts and no motor changes. ⚠️ Firmware must not drive 12/13/15/16 as GPIOs once the codec is enabled. NuttX side: `nuttx/drivers/audio/es8311.c` supports `AUDIO_TYPE_INPUT`, and `esp32s3_i2s.c` has `i2s_receive()` with `CONFIG_ESP32S3_I2S0_RX` default y. No ASR engine exists in the tree — keyword spotting would be TFLM, or cloud via `external/bailian_sdk`.

92	## Feeder dispensing — grams -> motion (calibration)
93	The app speaks **grams** (portions ~5-50g, daily limits 20-300g; NOT kg). The dispenser does not measure grams; it is CALIBRATED once:
94	- Measure kibble released per unit of motion: run the auger 1 rotation (or motor 1 s), weigh the output on a kitchen scale -> e.g. `grams_per_rotation` ~= 5g (or `grams_per_second` ~= 8g). Store the constant (NVS/SD so it survives reboot).
95	- **Dispense N grams = run actuator for N / grams_per_unit** (e.g. 20g @ 5g/rot = 4 rotations, or 2.5s @ 8g/s).
96	- This is OPEN-LOOP feeding (no sensor): ~±10-20% accurate, standard for consumer feeders. Fine for v1.

[Backup] If asked why this board. We started on Espressif's ESP32-S3-EYE, which has the same chip. Its 1.3-inch screen was too small for the feeding interface, and it has no touch, no clock chip and no speaker. The Waveshare 3.5-inch board adds a capacitive touch screen, a PCF85063 real-time clock for meal times, an ES8311 codec with a mic and speaker for voice, a connector for the 5-megapixel OV5640, and 16 MB of flash. We brought the board up on NuttX ourselves: LCD, camera, audio, clock and USB networking.

11	VelaPaw **Trends tab** reworked to match a shared product mockup, running on the ESP32-S3 (2026-07-21). Three stacked cards, all in `app/velapaw/ui/ui_lvgl.c` (build_trends/refresh_trends + helpers). Bilingual via [[velapaw-i18n]]. Confirmed good on the panel ("perfect").
12	
13	## What's there
14	1. **Colored intake bars** — the existing `lv_chart` BAR, recolored per-bar: green if that day >= the window average, blue if below (the colour split IS the baseline, so no separate average line). Avg is computed over **completed days only** (exclude today = last index; today is often 0 g and would drag the mean so every past day reads above-average = all green).
15	2. **Appetite trend** — a second `lv_chart` LINE card: each day's intake as % of the pet's `daily_limit_g` (0-100), COL_ACCENT line.
16	3. **BCS gauge** — a 3-zone semicircular dial: three `lv_arc` bands (amber Under 180-240°, green Ideal 240-300°, red Over 300-360°; LVGL arc 0°=3 o'clock, CW, so 180-360 = top half) + an `lv_line` needle + a hub. GA_D=150, arc width 18, needle width 7 **white** for a real reading / grey for "no reading", white-ringed hub, big class label below. Needle tip offsets are hardcoded per class (only 3 classes) — no trig/math.h: under=(-54,-31), ideal=(0,-62), over=(54,-31), NA=(0,-36).
17	
18	## LVGL 9.1 API gotchas (each cost a cycle — the console is dead during any wedge, so it's build+flash+eyeball only)
19	- **Per-bar chart colour**: use the `LV_EVENT_DRAW_TASK_ADDED` event + `lv_obj_add_flag(chart, LV_OBJ_FLAG_SEND_DRAW_TASK_EVENTS)`. In 9.1 read the base dsc via **`task->draw_dsc`** (the getter `lv_draw_task_get_draw_dsc()` is **9.2-only** → undefined reference at link). `lv_draw_task_get_fill_dsc()` DOES exist in 9.1. The point index is **`base->id1`** (NOT id2 — id2 is the series index; with a single series id2 is always 0 → every bar reads vals[0] → all one colour).
20	- **No `lv_meter`** in 9.x. `lv_scale` exists and `lv_scale_set_line_needle_value` IS in 9.1, but the section range/style setters are NOT (they're later) — so I built the coloured zones from stacked `lv_arc` instead of lv_scale sections.
21	- Forward-declare `refresh_bcs_gauge` before refresh_trends (it's defined after, but called by it).
22	
23	## Data note
24	BCS (`velapaw_store_get_bcs`) is a 3-class score set only when a pet is **recognized** (the 2nd model majority-votes). Empty demo data → gauge shows grey "-" (no reading). To demo the needle swinging, recognize a pet on the Recognize tab first. No per-day BCS history is stored, so the mockup's little BCS sparkline was NOT built.

output: 43	  <aside>[0:30 · ends 1:15] This is the core of VelaPaw. Food drops only when two answers agree. Who: the camera and an on-device model decide whether this is an enrolled pet, and a match needs a cosine score of at least 0.45. When: is this pet's own meal due, and not yet fed today? Only when both say yes does it dispense that pet's portion, once per meal per day, and any meal slot can be skipped. In this photo bob scored 0.63, meal 1 of 3 was due, and he got 15 grams. A stranger, or bob coming back for seconds, gets nothing.</aside>

54	  <aside>[0:20 · ends 1:35] This is a complete prototype, not a bare dev board. A 28BYJ-48 stepper turns a paddle rotor under the hopper and carries kibble round to the bowl. Our first design used a servo, but it only swung back and forth, and with the inlet and outlet 180 degrees apart, kibble never got through. The enclosure is 3D-printed.</aside>

51	  <aside>[1:40 · ends 3:15] Now the live demo. Our test pets are printed photos, because the university doesn't allow live pets. (1) Hold bob's photo in front of the camera: the screen shows bob and his score, Fed 15 grams, and you hear the rotor turn. (2) Show bob again: no food, because meal 1 is already fed today. (3) Show a cat that was never enrolled: no match, no food. (4) Open Trends: today's 15 of 60 grams, the appetite line and the body-condition gauge. (5) Only if the laptop's internet sharing is up: type ask set bob's dinner to 19:15 at the console. A toast appears under the bell and My Pets redraws with 19:15. Use a fresh sentence every time; the same question within five minutes is answered from cache. (6) Optional, if the hall is quiet: tap to talk and say two, eight, yes, then tap Save. Meal 2 is set to 08:00 with no network at all. If anything misbehaves, switch to the recorded run and keep talking.</aside>

96	  <aside>[0:30 · ends 3:45] Everything you just saw is one loop on one ESP32-S3. The camera frame becomes an embedding, matched against every enrolled pet; a stranger gets nothing. For a known pet, the gate asks: is its meal due and not yet fed? If not, the screen shows the next meal. If yes, the stepper dispenses 15 grams, and the meal is logged for Trends and in status.md, which the agent checks every 30 minutes. Only the agent needs the internet. (Not to read aloud: meal times come from touch, offline voice or the agent; the bottom strip is how we build it, from training the models on a PC to flashing over USB.)</aside>

117	  <aside>[0:25 · ends 4:10] Here is the stack on that one chip. We brought the Waveshare board up on NuttX ourselves: the LCD and camera over DMA, I2S audio, the clock, and USB networking for the agent. On top sit openVela's tflite-micro with Espressif's ESP-NN kernels, LVGL 9, the ai_agent and littlefs. The 16 MB flash holds the firmware, a data partition, both models as raw images, and the enrolled pets with their photos.</aside>

65	  <aside>[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.</aside>

68	  <aside>[0:30 · ends 5:25] Meal times can also be set by voice, with no network at all. In a pet's edit screen, one tap starts a three-step dialog: which meal, which hour, then confirm. Each step listens only for its own words. These are the console lines from a real run on the board: two, eight, yes, and meal 2 is set to 08:00 in 9.6 seconds with no false accepts. Two choices keep it safe. We threshold the raw score and never renormalise over the allowed words: renormalising let 86 percent of silence and stray words through the yes-or-no step, while the raw score lets 4.9 percent through. And a word heard twice above 0.25 is accepted, which rescued real dialogs like this hour step. The result goes into the edit dialog, so the owner still taps Save.</aside>

43	  <aside>[0:40 · ends 6:05] The second AI layer is openVela's ai_agent, on the same chip. Left, photographed on the board: set bob's breakfast to 07:45. The agent changed the meal with set_meal_schedule, a tool we added, and the screen confirmed it. A typical run is two tool calls in about five seconds, DeepSeek over TLS from the board. Right: it also acts unasked. The 30-minute check-in flagged bob, who had not been fed that day. To make it reliable we cut 20 unused tool schemas, so each request fits the 12.5-kilobyte buffer pool: 8 of 8 runs completed. Only the agent needs the internet; feeding never does.</aside>

43	  <aside>[0:30 · ends 1:15] This is the core of VelaPaw. Food drops only when two answers agree. Who: the camera and an on-device model decide whether this is an enrolled pet, and a match needs a cosine score of at least 0.45. When: is this pet's own meal due, and not yet fed today? Only when both say yes does it dispense that pet's portion, once per meal per day, and any meal slot can be skipped. In this photo bob scored 0.63, meal 1 of 3 was due, and he got 15 grams. A stranger, or bob coming back for seconds, gets nothing.</aside>

54	  <aside>[0:20 · ends 1:35] This is a complete prototype, not a bare dev board. A 28BYJ-48 stepper turns a paddle rotor under the hopper and carries kibble round to the bowl. Our first design used a servo, but it only swung back and forth, and with the inlet and outlet 180 degrees apart, kibble never got through. The enclosure is 3D-printed.</aside>

51	  <aside>[1:40 · ends 3:15] Now the live demo. Our test pets are printed photos, because the university doesn't allow live pets. (1) Hold bob's photo in front of the camera: the screen shows bob and his score, Fed 15 grams, and you hear the rotor turn. (2) Show bob again: no food, because meal 1 is already fed today. (3) Show a cat that was never enrolled: no match, no food. (4) Open Trends: today's 15 of 60 grams, the appetite line and the body-condition gauge. (5) Only if the laptop's internet sharing is up: type ask set bob's dinner to 19:15 at the console. A toast appears under the bell and My Pets redraws with 19:15. Use a fresh sentence every time; the same question within five minutes is answered from cache. (6) Optional, if the hall is quiet: tap to talk and say two, eight, yes, then tap Save. Meal 2 is set to 08:00 with no network at all. If anything misbehaves, switch to the recorded run and keep talking.</aside>

96	  <aside>[0:30 · ends 3:45] Everything you just saw is one loop on one ESP32-S3. The camera frame becomes an embedding, matched against every enrolled pet; a stranger gets nothing. For a known pet, the gate asks: is its meal due and not yet fed? If not, the screen shows the next meal. If yes, the stepper dispenses 15 grams, and the meal is logged for Trends and in status.md, which the agent checks every 30 minutes. Only the agent needs the internet. (Not to read aloud: meal times come from touch, offline voice or the agent; the bottom strip is how we build it, from training the models on a PC to flashing over USB.)</aside>

117	  <aside>[0:25 · ends 4:10] Here is the stack on that one chip. We brought the Waveshare board up on NuttX ourselves: the LCD and camera over DMA, I2S audio, the clock, and USB networking for the agent. On top sit openVela's tflite-micro with Espressif's ESP-NN kernels, LVGL 9, the ai_agent and littlefs. The 16 MB flash holds the firmware, a data partition, both models as raw images, and the enrolled pets with their photos.</aside>

65	  <aside>[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.</aside>

68	  <aside>[0:30 · ends 5:25] Meal times can also be set by voice, with no network at all. In a pet's edit screen, one tap starts a three-step dialog: which meal, which hour, then confirm. Each step listens only for its own words. These are the console lines from a real run on the board: two, eight, yes, and meal 2 is set to 08:00 in 9.6 seconds with no false accepts. Two choices keep it safe. We threshold the raw score and never renormalise over the allowed words: renormalising let 86 percent of silence and stray words through the yes-or-no step, while the raw score lets 4.9 percent through. And a word heard twice above 0.25 is accepted, which rescued real dialogs like this hour step. The result goes into the edit dialog, so the owner still taps Save.</aside>

43	  <aside>[0:40 · ends 6:05] The second AI layer is openVela's ai_agent, on the same chip. Left, photographed on the board: set bob's breakfast to 07:45. The agent changed the meal with set_meal_schedule, a tool we added, and the screen confirmed it. A typical run is two tool calls in about five seconds, DeepSeek over TLS from the board. Right: it also acts unasked. The 30-minute check-in flagged bob, who had not been fed that day. To make it reliable we cut 20 unused tool schemas, so each request fits the 12.5-kilobyte buffer pool: 8 of 8 runs completed. Only the agent needs the internet; feeding never does.</aside>

Made for homes with more than one pet

2026 首届 openvela AI 硬件开发者大赛

目标用户与使用场景：家里养了多只宠物，每只的食量和饭点各不相同；录入宠物并设好饭点后，喂食就交给 VelaPaw。

HOW AN OWNER USES IT

1 · SET UP ONCE

Enrol each pet

5 photos, no retraining

Its own portion, daily cap and up to 3 meal times

2 · EVERY MEAL

The right pet eats

Food only for a known pet whose meal is due

Change times by touch, voice or one sentence

3 · EVERY DAY

Spot a pet eating less

Appetite trends, and an alert when it drops

Body condition: an AI estimate, not a diagnosis

BUILT IN

A daily cap per pet, never exceeded

Feeds with no network, phone or account

Camera frames never leave the board

English / 中文 interface, switched live

(Not to read aloud: meal times can also be changed by voice or with one sentence to the agent; feeding needs no network, phone or account; camera frames never leave the board; the body-condition score is shown as an AI estimate, not a diagnosis.)

PROJECT DEFENSE · 项目答辩

Made for homes with more than one pet

2026 首届 openvela AI 硬件开发者大赛

目标用户与使用场景：家里养了多只宠物，每只的食量和饭点各不相同；录入宠物并设好饭点后，喂食就交给 VelaPaw。

HOW AN OWNER USES IT

1 · SET UP ONCE

Enrol each pet

5 photos, no retraining

Its own portion, daily cap and up to 3 meal times

2 · EVERY MEAL

The right pet eats

Food only for a known pet whose meal is due

Change times by touch, voice or one sentence

3 · EVERY DAY

Spot a pet eating less

Appetite trends, and an alert when it drops

Body condition: an AI estimate, not a diagnosis

BUILT IN

A daily cap per pet, never exceeded

Feeds with no network, phone or account

Camera frames never leave the board

English / 中文 interface, switched live

[0:25 · ends 1:10] Who is it for? Homes with two or more pets on different diets. The owner enrols each pet with five photos, then sets its portion, a daily cap and up to three meal times. From then on VelaPaw feeds the right pet at the right time, and shows an alert when a pet's appetite drops. (Not to read aloud: meal times can also be changed by voice or with one sentence to the agent; feeding needs no network, phone or account; camera frames never leave the board; the body-condition score is shown as an AI estimate, not a diagnosis.)

input.old_string: <aside>[0:45 · ends 4:55] Recognition is open-set metric learning, so the model never learned bob. It turns a 128 by 128 crop into a 128-number fingerprint, an L2-normalised embedding. Enrolling a pet stores five of these, and recognition is a cosine comparison against them, so adding a pet needs no retraining. The network is MobileNetV3-Small with a TSFM spatial-attention block, quantised to INT8. The attention block widened the margin between pets by a third, 0.324 against 0.243, and lowered the equal error rate from 0.328 to 0.291. With Espressif's ESP-NN kernels one recognition takes about 1.3 seconds instead of 6.75, and it runs on a background worker so the screen never freezes. We match at 0.45: bob scores between 0.53 and 0.84, and unknown cats stay at or below 0.22. The biggest lever against false accepts is good enrollment photos.</aside>

These are the console lines from a real run on the board: two, eight, yes, and meal 2 is set to 08:00 in 9.6 seconds with no false accepts. Two choices keep it safe. We threshold the raw score and never renormalise over the allowed words: renormalising let 86 percent of silence and stray words through the yes-or-no step, while the raw score lets 4.9 percent through. 38	1. **`recog_done` latch** — after one match or 2 misses, Recognize waited for a tab re-entry; looks exactly like "fails to recognize". stab1 re-arms on a tap, on a scene change (4×4 brightness signature), and once a minute while a meal is due (its first 30 min); gap 30 s after a hit, 3 s doubling to 20 s after misses.
39	2. **Console jam** — `uart_write` takes `xmit.lock` BEFORE it checks O_NONBLOCK, so one blocking writer + a host that stopped draining COM8 (PuTTY closed, PC asleep) jams every writer, UI thread included. stab1: `uprintf` (UI) and `vp_say` (store) ask FIONSPACE first (answered under a spinlock) and drop the line instead (counted as `drop`). Rejected: a pipe relay (CONFIG_PIPES off) and a dup2 mute.
40	3. Midnight: `today_total` wasn't reconciled for a board running past midnight → a day that ended at the cap refused the next day's meals. Fix: `velapaw_store_sync_day()` on the UI's day change.

Fed/skip flags were RAM-only → a reset could re-serve an eaten meal. 11. `g_last_fed` was never read → no gap between two due meals. 12. The limit-hit path left stale `fed_min`/`fed_g`.

43	## Design decisions worth keeping
44	- **At-most-once feeding:** `/data/ai_agent/velapaw/fed.bin` (magic `VPF1`, via `velapaw_store_put/get`) is saved BEFORE the dispense; `FEED_GAP_MIN` 20; a slot closed by the daily limit shows "skipped"; skips restore only on the same day.
45	- **Stall monitor:** a prio+10 thread (2 KB stack) watches the UI heartbeat (2 min; 10 min while the tag is `feed`) and the recognition worker (1 min). A prio+5 note thread (6 KB) writes `STALL <kind> at <tag> <age>s | <health line>` to flash, then `up_systemreset()` (reset code 0x03); it waits at most 3 s for the note. Started right before the main loop. **Not a HW watchdog** — an interrupts-off hang isn't caught.
46	- **health.log** = `/data/ai_agent/velapaw/health.log`, rotates at 4 KB into `health.old`. Boot line `HH:MM boot rst 0xNN`; every 10 min `HH:MM up Nm tab T cap N max Nms slow N same N err N embed N hit N miss N inf S drop N`. `velapaw voice` (read-only probe) prints the live line + the boot code.
47	- **There is NO software-reset command in this build:** `reboot` → `nsh: reboot: command not found` (2026-10-18), probably because `CONFIG_BOARDCTL_RESET` is off. **Don't suggest ai_agent's `restart`**: without BOARDCTL_RESET it prints "Restarting..." and sleeps forever, which parks the agent CLI. The RESET button gives 0x01, so the 0x03 → start-on-Recognize path can only be exercised by a real stall.
48	- Reset codes (`esp32s3_reset_reasons(0)`): 0x01 power-on/brown-out/RESET button, **0x03 CORE_SW = the stall monitor's `up_systemreset()`**, 0x07/0x08 MWDT, 0x09 RTC WDT, 0x0f brown-out, 0x15/0x16 USB UART/JTAG (esptool). Any other code than 0x01/0x15/0x16, with pets enrolled, boots on Recognize.
49	- Never patch `ui_i18n.c` — stab1 reuses `S_POINT_AT_PET`, `S_NEXT_MEAL_FMT`, `S_SKIPPED`.
50	
51	## Gotchas
52	- All velapaw sources are **LF** — an in-session note that said CRLF was wrong.
53	- No LVGL heap metric (`CONFIG_LV_USE_CLIB_MALLOC=y`) and a heap walk kills the board ([[velapaw-heap-walk-kills-board]]).
54	- Thread stacks come from IMEM (~64 KB headroom before stab1's 8 KB).
55	- Pre-existing VM warnings outside the patched files — ignore: `ui_i18n.c:245` `f14` set but not used; `agent_loop.c:740` `-Wformat-truncation`.
56	- Local compile check: `cc_check.sh <a|b> <file>` = arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.4 after `source /d/openVela/vela-env.sh`, flags from `compile_commands.json`, item8/b headers (`identity.h` 564256ad, `ui_i18n.h` 778b1a32). The VM is xtensa GCC 12.2, so the VM warning gate is the real check.
57	- Still-ungated prints (feeder, TFLM, BCS lazy init, identity, boot init, camera + LVGL syslog): a jam there now ends in a stall reset + a log line instead of a silent hang.
58	- A stall reset re-enumerates USB: reopen COM8, redo `ifconfig eth0 …`, ping to prime ARP ([[velapaw-cdcncm-networking]]).
59	
60	Offered, not done: HW watchdog (`CONFIG_WATCHDOG` + automonitor), `CONFIG_BOARD_RESET_ON_ASSERT`, syslog hardening, auto-ifconfig after a reset, idle return to Recognize, a camera HAL that returns -1 / re-inits. 3	description: "OV5640 camera orientation (90 deg rotation) and purple-tint color bug on VelaPaw hardware — root cause and the fix that shipped, confirmed working on hardware 2026-08-09"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project

10	
11	**SOLVED + SHIPPED 2026-08-09.** VelaPaw's Enroll-tab camera preview had two bugs that looked related but weren't: an orientation bug (image rotated) and a color bug (purple tint). Both are now fixed and confirmed correct on real hardware (hand test: fingers-up renders fingers-up; color no longer purple).
12	
13	## Orientation: it was a 90 deg transpose, not a flip
14	
15	**Diagnostic trick that broke the case open:** hold a real hand up in front of the camera (fingers pointing up) and look at the preview. A **vertical→horizontal** result (fingers appearing sideways) can *only* come from a 90 deg rotation/transpose. Flip and mirror (the OV5640's `0x3820`/`0x3821` registers) can each only reverse one axis — neither, nor any combination, can ever turn vertical into horizontal. Chasing this with sensor flip/mirror registers is structurally unable to work; a color-bar test earlier in the debugging session had hinted at this (horizontal bars where vertical were expected) but got wrongly dismissed as a binning artifact.
16	
17	**Fix:** correct the rotation in software, in the HAL's downscale/resample step — `app/velapaw/hal/camera_ov5640.c`, in `velapaw_camera_get_frame()`. The old code was a plain resize + horizontal mirror. Determined the needed correction was **90 deg CW** by tracing where each output-image corner samples from in the raw 320x240 buffer (not by guessing — get this backwards and it's another flash cycle to find out). Final resample also folds in the existing selfie-mirror on the corrected (post-rotation) axis:
18	
19	```c
20	int dy = y * w / VELAPAW_FRAME_H;   /* w = CAM_W = 320 */
21	int sx = dy;
22	...
23	int mox = (VELAPAW_FRAME_W - 1) - x;
24	int dx = mox * h / VELAPAW_FRAME_W; /* h = CAM_H = 240 */
25	int sy = (h - 1) - dx;
26	const uint8_t *p = buf + ((size_t)sy * w + sx) * 2;
27	```
28	
29	**Important dependency:** this transpose is derived against whatever the sensor's raw output orientation is *at the time of the hand test*. If sensor-side flip/mirror registers (`0x3820`/`0x3821`) ever change again, the raw buffer's orientation changes too, and the hand test (and possibly the CW/CCW direction) needs to be redone. See [[velapaw-camera-connector]] for the physical mount/pinout side of the camera.
30	
31	## Color: the purple tint was from splitting OV5640's flip bits
32	
33	Earlier debugging assumed `0x3820`/`0x3821` bit1 = "sensor-side flip" (shifts Bayer CFA phase, causes purple) and bit2 = "ISP-side flip" (safe, post-debayer). Testing bit2-only (`0x05`/`0x05`) still produced the purple tint — that hypothesis was wrong. In the OV5640 (per standard reference driver code, e.g. esp32-camera's `ov5640.c`), **bits 1 and 2 are meant to be toggled together as one flip unit (mask `0x06`)**, not used as independent safe/unsafe halves — setting bit2 alone leaves the sensor in an undefined partial-flip state.
34	
35	**Fix:** since software now owns 100% of the orientation correction (see above), there's no need for the sensor to flip/mirror at all. Cleared bits 1+2 entirely, preserving whatever bit0 was for (unknown purpose, untouched, was already `1` in the working baseline): `ov5640_wr(i,0x3820,0x01);ov5640_wr(i,0x3821,0x01);` (board file, `ov5640_config_qvga()`). Do not reintroduce `0x3820`/`0x3821` bit1 or bit2 without re-testing color — that combination is the confirmed cause.
36	
37	## Purple round 2 — the REAL other half was `0x4514` (SOLVED 2026-09-05)
38	
39	The tint came back on the ai_agent builds. The flip-bit fix above was intact and genuinely compiled in — this was a **different register on the same source line**. `0x4514` is the OV5640's **BLC (black-level calibration) pattern**, and its value is not free: it must match the Bayer phase the flip/mirror bits select. The standard pairing (Linux `ov5640` driver, esp32-camera):
40	
41	- mirror **on** (`0x3821` bits 1+2 set) → `0x4514 = 0xbb`
42	- mirror **off** (`0x3821` bits cleared) → `0x4514 = 0x88`
43	
44	The shipped line cleared the mirror bits but left `0x4514` at `0xbb` — the *mirrored* BLC pattern. Black-level offsets then get subtracted from the wrong colour cells. **Fixed line:** `ov5640_wr(i,0x3820,0x01);ov5640_wr(i,0x3821,0x01);ov5640_wr(i,0x4514,0x88);` — confirmed perfect on hardware 2026-09-05, md5 `4bfb6733d77bac88fb1e2d6e9ded5dee`. Whenever `0x3821`'s flip bits change, change `0x4514` with them.
45	
46	**The symptom tells you which of the two it is, and it's decisive:** a flip/Bayer-phase error *exchanges* red and blue and leaves green alone (green is 2 of 4 Bayer cells either way) — it physically cannot cause green loss. A BLC-pattern mismatch crushes a channel: the frame goes violet/magenta (R+B, no G) while the LCD's own UI chrome stays perfectly coloured. **Judge from the whole frame's hue, not from a red/blue swap test** — chasing the flip bits when green is missing wastes hours.
47	
48	**Do NOT verify with a byte scan of `nuttx.bin`** — see the correction in [[velapaw-b82-camerafix-rebuild]]. Those registers are separate `ov5640_wr()` calls, so the register number sits in an Xtensa literal pool and the value is a `movi.n` immediate; they are never adjacent bytes.
49	
50	Do not run `rebuild_camera_fix.sh` when the board file has local edits — it `wget`s `esp32s3_st7789.c` from the Windows server on :9100 and overwrites it.
51	
52	## Workflow note
53	
54	Rebuild/reflash loop: VM has no sshd, so Windows serves source files via `python -m http.server` (repo root on :9100) and the VM pulls, rebuilds, and serves `nuttx.bin` back on :8000. **VM's own IP is 192.168.160.128; the Windows host (as seen from the VM) is 192.168.160.1** — these are easy to swap by mistake (a script inherited from earlier in a session had `WIN_HOST` set to the VM's own IP, which fails every pull silently until checked with `ipconfig` for the VMnet8 adapter). Flashing consistently needs the manual BOOT-hold + RESET-tap dance done *while `esptool` is actively retrying* (not before) — auto-reset via DTR/RTS is unreliable on this board; a `Write timeout` from a plain `write-flash` almost always means the chip wasn't actually in bootloader mode yet, not a driver problem (verified: raw pyserial writes to the port succeed fine even while esptool's handshake fails).
