### Skill: artifact-design
Path: bundled:artifact-design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# kconfig-tweak

Command-line tool for modifying `.config` files without launching interactive menuconfig.

## Quick Reference

```bash
# Enable/disable options
kconfig-tweak --enable DEBUG_INFO
kconfig-tweak --disable MODULES
kconfig-tweak -e SMP -d PREEMPT    # Multiple in one command

# Set values
kconfig-tweak --set-val LOG_BUF_SHIFT 17
kconfig-tweak --set-str LOCALVERSION "-custom"

# Query state
kconfig-tweak --state DEBUG_INFO   # Returns: y, n, m, or undef

# Specify config file
kconfig-tweak --file boards/myboard/.config --enable USB

# Module support
kconfig-tweak --module DRM         # Set to m (module)
```

## Commands

| Command | Short | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--enable OPTION` | `-e` | Set option to y |
| `--disable OPTION` | `-d` | Set option to n |
| `--module OPTION` | `-m` | Set option to m (module) |
| `--set-val OPTION VALUE` | - | Set integer/hex value |
| `--set-str OPTION STRING` | - | Set string value (quoted) |
| `--undefine OPTION` | `-u` | Remove option definition |
| `--state OPTION` | `-s` | Query current state |

## Position Control

Insert options after a specific option (useful for maintaining config order):

```bash
kconfig-tweak --enable-after USB USB_STORAGE    # -E
kconfig-tweak --disable-after NET BRIDGE        # -D
kconfig-tweak --module-after DRM DRM_I915       # -M
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--file FILE` | Target config file (default: .config) |
| `--keep-case` / `-k` | Preserve symbol case (default: auto-uppercase) |

## Environment Variables

- `CONFIG_` - Symbol prefix (default: "CONFIG_")

## Common Patterns

### Batch Configuration
```bash
# Enable multiple debug options
kconfig-tweak -e DEBUG_INFO -e DEBUG_FS -e KALLSYMS

# Configure network stack
kconfig-tweak --file .config \
  -e NET -e INET -e IPV6 \
  --set-val TCP_CONG_CUBIC y
```

### CI/CD Integration
```bash
# Start from defconfig, then customize
make defconfig
kconfig-tweak -e DEBUG_INFO -d MODULES
make olddefconfig  # Resolve dependencies
```

### Query Before Modify
```bash
# Check current state
STATE=$(kconfig-tweak -s PREEMPT)
if [ "$STATE" = "y" ]; then
  kconfig-tweak -d PREEMPT
fi
```

## Notes

- kconfig-tweak does NOT validate dependencies; run `make olddefconfig` after modifications
- Symbol names auto-uppercase unless `--keep-case` is used
- Changes are immediate; no confirmation prompt

Nothing is broken: this is the feeder's 20-minute rule. It always leaves at least 20 minutes between two meals for the same pet, counted from when Bob actually ate, not from the time you set. Bob ate the 07:55 meal at 08:03 (board time), so the 08:10 meal is held until 08:03 + 20 = **08:23**.

The "Next meal" message only ever shows one of two things: a meal's set time, or the end of that 20-minute wait. 08:23 isn't one of Bob's meal times, so it's the wait. To confirm, the last line of the feed log should show a meal at 08:03:

```
cat /data/ai_agent/velapaw/feed_log.md
```

**What to do now:** leave the board on the Recognize screen with Bob in front of the camera. The camera keeps checking once a minute until 08:39, so the 08:10 meal comes out by itself at about 08:23. If Bob isn't there then, tap the screen any time after 08:23. If you need food out sooner, a voice "yes" feed isn't held by the wait, but it adds a portion on top of the scheduled meals.

**Why 08:10 is too early:**
- After a plug-in the clock starts at 08:00, so the 07:55 meal can't come out before 08:00.
- That means the next meal can't come before 08:20. With it set at 08:10, the screen will show a later time every time.
- Set it to 08:25 or later. Then, as long as Bob eats the first meal by 08:05, the second comes out at the time you set.
- You can change it now. The meal Bob already ate stays marked as eaten, so nothing comes out twice.

**Optional tidy-up:** the screen numbers meals by their slot, not by time. Right now the 07:55 meal is the second meal but comes out first. Setting the first meal to 07:55 and the second to 08:25 puts the numbers in order.

A timer can't tell two cats apart

2026 首届 openvela AI 硬件开发者大赛

定时喂食器分不清是哪只宠物：抢得快的吃两份，胆小的挨饿，每只都喂一样多，食欲下降也没人发现。

The fastest pet eats it all

A timer drops food at 08:00 for whoever gets there first. The bold cat eats twice; the shy one goes hungry.

Same scoop for every pet

A kitten, a senior on a diet and a cat on prescription food all get the same portion at the same time.

Appetite drops go unseen

Eating less is often the first sign of illness. A feeder that can't tell who ate can't tell who stopped.

结论

VelaPaw feeds the pet, not the clock.

Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# kconfig-tweak

Command-line tool for modifying `.config` files without launching interactive menuconfig.

## Quick Reference

```bash
# Enable/disable options
kconfig-tweak --enable DEBUG_INFO
kconfig-tweak --disable MODULES
kconfig-tweak -e SMP -d PREEMPT    # Multiple in one command

# Set values
kconfig-tweak --set-val LOG_BUF_SHIFT 17
kconfig-tweak --set-str LOCALVERSION "-custom"

# Query state
kconfig-tweak --state DEBUG_INFO   # Returns: y, n, m, or undef

# Specify config file
kconfig-tweak --file boards/myboard/.config --enable USB

# Module support
kconfig-tweak --module DRM         # Set to m (module)
```

## Commands

| Command | Short | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| `--enable OPTION` | `-e` | Set option to y |
| `--disable OPTION` | `-d` | Set option to n |
| `--module OPTION` | `-m` | Set option to m (module) |
| `--set-val OPTION VALUE` | - | Set integer/hex value |
| `--set-str OPTION STRING` | - | Set string value (quoted) |
| `--undefine OPTION` | `-u` | Remove option definition |
| `--state OPTION` | `-s` | Query current state |

## Position Control

Insert options after a specific option (useful for maintaining config order):

```bash
kconfig-tweak --enable-after USB USB_STORAGE    # -E
kconfig-tweak --disable-after NET BRIDGE        # -D
kconfig-tweak --module-after DRM DRM_I915       # -M
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--file FILE` | Target config file (default: .config) |
| `--keep-case` / `-k` | Preserve symbol case (default: auto-uppercase) |

## Environment Variables

- `CONFIG_` - Symbol prefix (default: "CONFIG_")

## Common Patterns

### Batch Configuration
```bash
# Enable multiple debug options
kconfig-tweak -e DEBUG_INFO -e DEBUG_FS -e KALLSYMS

# Configure network stack
kconfig-tweak --file .config \
  -e NET -e INET -e IPV6 \
  --set-val TCP_CONG_CUBIC y
```

### CI/CD Integration
```bash
# Start from defconfig, then customize
make defconfig
kconfig-tweak -e DEBUG_INFO -d MODULES
make olddefconfig  # Resolve dependencies
```

### Query Before Modify
```bash
# Check current state
STATE=$(kconfig-tweak -s PREEMPT)
if [ "$STATE" = "y" ]; then
  kconfig-tweak -d PREEMPT
fi
```

## Notes

- kconfig-tweak does NOT validate dependencies; run `make olddefconfig` after modifications
- Symbol names auto-uppercase unless `--keep-case` is used
- Changes are immediate; no confirmation prompt

[Backup] If asked why this board. We started on Espressif's ESP32-S3-EYE, which has the same chip. Its 1.3-inch screen was too small for the feeding interface, and it has no touch, no clock chip and no speaker. The Waveshare 3.5-inch board adds a capacitive touch screen, a PCF85063 real-time clock for meal times, an ES8311 codec with a mic and speaker for voice, a connector for the 5-megapixel OV5640, and 16 MB of flash. We brought the board up on NuttX ourselves: LCD, camera, audio, clock and USB networking.

[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. The panel's chip-select is tied low, so one stray clock edge at the pin handover desynchronised it; a reset after the handover fixed it, and it now runs at 40 MHz with DMA. The rest are on the table: a static-init deadlock, a mic DMA alignment stall, an agent stack in PSRAM, and overlapping USB FIFOs.

[0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. [0:30 · ends 6:55] One story in full: the screen drew nothing over hardware SPI. After about 60 builds, a 45-yuan logic analyzer showed the bytes on the wire were perfect. 为什么用步进电机：舵机只能来回摆动，而进料口和出料口相隔 180°，粮食始终送不过去。步进电机能让拨轮整圈旋转，把粮带到出料口。

带动料仓下方的拨轮

为饭点计时 · 语音用的麦克风和扬声器

3D 打印外壳

料仓、拨轮仓、屏幕支架和摄像头立杆

[0:20 · ends 2:00] This is a complete prototype, not a bare dev board. A 28BYJ-48 stepper turns a paddle rotor under the hopper and carries kibble round to the bowl. Our first design used a servo, but it only swung back and forth, and with the inlet and outlet 180 degrees apart, kibble never got through. The enclosure is 3D-printed.

[1:40 · ends 3:40] Now the live demo. Our test pets are printed photos, because the university doesn't allow live pets. (1) Hold bob's photo in front of the camera: the screen shows bob and his score, Fed 15 grams, and you hear the rotor turn. (2) Show bob again: no food, because meal 1 is already fed today. (3) Show a cat that was never enrolled: no match, no food. (4) Open Trends: today's 15 of 60 grams, the appetite line and the body-condition gauge. (5) Only if the laptop's internet sharing is up: type ask set bob's dinner to 19:15 at the console. A toast appears under the bell and My Pets redraws with 19:15. Use a fresh sentence every time; the same question within five minutes is answered from cache. (6) Optional, if the hall is quiet: tap to talk and say two, eight, yes, then tap Save. Meal 2 is set to 08:00 with no network at all. If anything misbehaves, switch to the recorded run and keep talking.

[0:30 · ends 4:10] Everything you just saw is one loop on one ESP32-S3. The camera frame becomes an embedding, matched against every enrolled pet; a stranger gets nothing. For a known pet, the gate asks: is its meal due and not yet fed? If not, the screen shows the next meal. If yes, the stepper dispenses 15 grams, and the meal is logged for Trends and in status.md, which the agent checks every 30 minutes. Only the agent needs the internet. (Not to read aloud: meal times come from touch, offline voice or the agent; the bottom strip is how we build it, from training the models on a PC to flashing over USB.)

[Backup] If asked why this board. We started on Espressif's ESP32-S3-EYE, which has the same chip. Its 1.3-inch screen was too small for the feeding interface, and it has no touch, no clock chip and no speaker. The Waveshare 3.5-inch board adds a capacitive touch screen, a PCF85063 real-time clock for meal times, an ES8311 codec with a mic and speaker for voice, a connector for the 5-megapixel OV5640, and 16 MB of flash. We brought the board up on NuttX ourselves: LCD, camera, audio, clock and USB networking.

断网时喂食照常进行，只有智能体需要等网络恢复。

[Backup] If asked what happens without a network. Everything that feeds the pets runs on the board: recognition, the feeding gate, meal schedules and daily caps, voice, trends and body condition, with pets, photos and schedules saved on flash. Only the agent needs the internet: the ask command and the 30-minute check-in. What it sends is text, your request plus the feeder's status such as pet names, meal times and intake; camera frames never leave the board. If the network drops, feeding carries on and only the agent waits.

11	The VelaPaw feeder's **28BYJ-48 + ULN2003 finally rotates** (2026-07-23). Coils: IN1=GPIO9, IN2=GPIO10, IN3=GPIO11, **IN4=GPIO43** (was 44).
12	
13	**Root cause of the long "vibrates but shaft won't turn" saga:** IN4 on **GPIO44 (U0RXD)** stayed clamped high even after re-asserting `esp32s3_configgpio(pin, OUTPUT)` before every dispense — the UART0 re-mux wins over the GPIO reclaim on that pin. Moving IN4 to **GPIO43 (U0TXD)** fixed it instantly; shaft turns on the first feed.
14	
15	**Second root cause, found 2026-08-02 from the schematic netlist:** the pre-bring-up code had IN1/IN2/IN3 on **GPIO12/13/15**, which are the ES8311 codec's I²S lines and are **not routed to the J8 header at all** (each net has exactly two nodes: ESP32 + codec). So for part of the saga three of the four coils were electrically unconnected — no coil-order table could ever have worked. Moving them to 9/10/11 (the unused microSD pins, the board's only reusable native GPIOs) is what made all four coils real. See [[velapaw-hardware]] for the full J8 map.
16	
17	**Why:** we burned many build/flash cycles chasing coil-order tables. Don't. The straight full-step table `{0x3,0x6,0xC,0x9}` (bit0=IN1..bit3=IN4) is the correct textbook 28BYJ-48 sequence. All 3 distinct coil-order topologies were swept and NONE turned — because the fault was one dead pin (44), not the sequence. A confident external "fix" to `{0x5,0x6,0xA,0x9}` was just re-proposing a sweep candidate we'd already tested.
18	
19	**How to apply:** keep IN4 on GPIO43. `feeder_pins_output()` (configgpio OUTPUT on all four) is still called at the start of `board_feeder_dispense` — harmless, keep it. STEP_PER_REV 2048 full-step, STEP_DELAY_US 3000 (~333 steps/s, within pull-in torque), one-direction ratchet.
20	
21	**Repo reconciled 2026-08-02.** The Windows repo copy of `board/esp32s3_st7789.c` had drifted badly from the VM: it carried a half-step table `k_halfstep[8]` (`STEP_PER_REV 4096`, `STEP_DELAY_US 1500`, `GRAMS_PER_POCKET 4`) with **bit3=IN1** — the *opposite* bit order to what runs. A rebuild from Windows would have turned the rotor backwards. Now matches the VM: full-step, `{0x3,0x6,0xC,0x9}`, bit0=IN1, 2048/3000µs/5g, plus `feeder_pins_output()` re-called at the top of `board_feeder_dispense`. See [[velapaw-golden-baseline]].
22	
23	**Still TODO:** (1) confirm rotation direction actually carries food inlet→outlet (reverse the phase index if backward); (2) calibrate `GRAMS_PER_POCKET` — currently placeholder 5, weigh one pocket; (3) add a fractional-step accumulator: 2048/6 = 341, and 341×6 = 2046, so straight integer pockets lose 2 steps/rev and the vane drifts over hundreds of dispenses.

32	## Feeder actuator: 28BYJ-48 stepper (switched from servo 2026-07-18)
33	**Why:** a code review caught a CRITICAL kinematic bug — inlet & outlet are 180° apart, and a servo can only OSCILLATE (zero net rotation), so a pocket filled at the inlet can never reach the outlet: it dispenses the initial charge a few times then **dead-heads forever** ("worst-case demo failure"). Confirmed in firmware (`rotor_index_one` swept 60° and back). A stepper rotates CONTINUOUSLY one direction → pockets ratchet inlet→outlet → true per-pocket dosing, and "grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET" becomes literally true. Geared 28BYJ-48 also has strong low-speed torque (resists kibble jams).
34	- **Firmware DONE** in `board/esp32s3_st7789.c`: replaced the LEDC servo with a ULN2003 half-step driver. `STEP_IN1..4 = GPIO 12/13/15/16` (ES8311 audio lines, free — no audio used, all ESP32→codec dirs). `STEP_PER_REV=4096` (28BYJ-48 half-step), `STEP_PER_POCKET=4096/6≈682`, `STEP_DELAY_US=1500`, `GRAMS_PER_POCKET=4`. `board_feeder_dispense` rotates `pockets × STEP_PER_POCKET` half-steps one way; coils de-energise at rest. Runs on the detached worker thread (busy-waits up_udelay). Board file must be rebuilt+flashed when the motor is wired (servo not attached yet).
35	- **5V bundle** (motor+ULN2003) runs off the SAME separate 5V ≥2A supply; common ground only.
36	- **MECHANICAL REDESIGN DONE (2026-07-18):** added `plate_stepper` (28BYJ-48 mount: Ø28 body bore + 2 flange holes 35mm apart, offset STEP_SHAFT_OFFS=8 from centre; replaces plate_servo which is kept as legacy) and changed the rotor's driven face to a **5mm double-D socket** (round∩slab). Params at top of .scad — ALL DATASHEET-CONFIRMED (5VDC unit): STEP_BODY_D=28, STEP_FLANGE_SPAN=35 (ears 42 t-t), STEP_SHAFT_D=5, STEP_SHAFT_FLAT=3, **STEP_SHAFT_LEN=8** (was 10, corrected from datasheet), STEP_BOSS_D=10, STEP_PER_REV=4096 (64:1). **5V CONFIRMED** (the 12V video was marketing). Legacy plate_servo.stl removed from stl/. assembly()/selector/notes repointed to plate_stepper. All render clean. **Verify STEP_SHAFT_FLAT + STEP_SHAFT_LEN with calipers before printing.** ⚠️ The listing's demo video showed a **12VDC** motor — CONFIRM the ordered unit is 5V (12V won't run on the 5V rail). housing/plate_idle/hopper/board_cradle unchanged.

41	## Bill of materials (to buy / print)
42	- Board: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C (camera+case included).
43	- **Servo (dispenser):** continuous-rotation micro servo **FS90R** (gentle, ~5V) driving a 3D-printed auger; or MG996R (more torque, needs its own supply). Single servo = single PWM pin.
44	- **Separate 5 V ≥2 A supply** for the servo + **~1000 µF cap** across it; common ground with the board. Do NOT power the servo from the board's 3.3V/LCD rail.
45	- **microSD card** (for persistent feed history).
46	- Jumper wires, M3 screws / heat-set inserts.
47	- **3D-printed (user has a print coupon):** hopper + lid, auger + tube, chute, bowl (or bowl mount), camera/board mount aiming the camera at the bowl, main enclosure.
48	
49	## Pinout — VERIFIED against the official ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5 schematic netlist (2026-08-02)
50	Native GPIO map:
51	- LCD (ST7796 SPI): IO1 MOSI, **IO3 DC**, **IO4 CS**, IO5 SCLK, IO6 BL. **IO2 is a DEAD PIN** — its net has exactly one node (the SoC). Waveshare never routed the display read-back line, and the LCD connector's SDO (L1.22) is dangling too. This is why the defconfig has `CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=-1`. IO2 is NOT on the header and cannot be used for anything.
52	- I2C bus (touch/RTC/IMU/audio codec/AXP/expander all shared): **IO7 SCL, IO8 SDA**
53	- microSD (SPI): IO9 MISO, IO10 MOSI, IO11 SCLK (SD_CS on expander EXIO3). **Slot is unused → these three are the board's only reusable native GPIOs, and the stepper now owns them.**
54	- I2S audio (ES8311): IO12 MCLK, IO13 SCLK, IO14 ASDOUT, IO15 LRCK, IO16 DSDIN. **PRIVATE BUS — not on any header.** Each net has exactly two nodes: ESP32 + codec. Nothing external can reach them, and nothing external can conflict with them.
55	- Camera (OV5640 DVP): IO17 VSYNC, IO18 HREF, IO21 D7, IO38 XCLK, IO39 D6, IO40 D5, IO41 PCLK, IO42 D4, IO45 D0, IO46 D3, IO47 D1, IO48 D2
56	- USB-C: IO19 (D-), IO20 (D+) — the console (USB-Serial/JTAG) rides here
57	- UART0: IO43 TXD (usable as GPIO), **IO44 RXD — clamped, will NOT drive an output** (the UART mux re-wins over `esp32s3_configgpio`)
58	- IO33–37 dangle (single-node nets); flash + octal PSRAM occupy the IO26–37 region internally
59	- IO0: IMU INT + strapping (avoid)
60	- TCA9554 expander EXIO0–7 (all used): CAM_PWDN, LCD_RST, TP_INT, SD_CS, RTC_INT, AXP_IRQ, SYS_OUT, PA_CTRL.
61	
62	## Header J8 (2×16, 2.54 mm) — the complete map
63	Odd column left, even right:
64	
65	| | | | |
66	|---|---|---|---|
67	| 1 VBAT | 2 VBUS | 17 IO45 | 18 IO18 |
68	| 3 GND | 4 GND | 19 IO46 | 20 IO0 |
69	| 5 IO21 | 6 USB_N | 21 IO47 | 22 EN |
70	| 7 IO38 | 8 USB_P | 23 IO48 | 24 PWRON |
71	| 9 IO39 | 10 **IO11** | 25 IO44 | 26 IO7 SCL |
72	| 11 IO40 | 12 **IO10** | 27 **IO43** | 28 IO8 SDA |
73	| 13 IO41 | 14 **IO9** | 29 GND | 30 GND |
74	| 15 IO42 | 16 IO17 | 31 3V3 | 32 3V3 |
75	
76	**No spare GPIOs remain.** Camera on J2 + stepper on 9/10/11/43 claims everything usable. Any new peripheral goes on the I²C bus (IO7/IO8) or through the TCA9554. An external I²S MEMS mic is **impossible** — there is nowhere to put it.
77	
78	## ACTUATOR WIRING (supersedes the old servo plan)
79	- **Stepper IN1/IN2/IN3/IN4 = GPIO 9/10/11/43** (J8 pins 14/12/10/27). See [[velapaw-stepper-bringup]].
80	- **Free IO43 by keeping the console on USB-Serial/JTAG** (IO19/20), never UART0. Full logging retained.
81	- **IO44 is not a usable output.** **IO12/13/15/16 reach the codec, not the header** — an early revision had IN1..IN3 there and three coils were simply unconnected (the buzz saga).
82	- **Motor power: separate 5 V ≥2 A + common ground** (see BOM). Flash/logs over USB-C.
83	- [Old servo-era note, now moot:] the expander was ruled out for a *servo* because I²C can't do µs-accurate 50 Hz PWM. That objection does not transfer to a stepper, which only needs ~667 coil updates/s (~4 % bus load at 400 kHz) — worth remembering if a pin ever has to be freed.
84	
85	## Onboard audio — free, costs zero GPIOs
86	The -C carries a **microphone** (analog differential into ES8311 `MIC1P`/`MIC1N` via R41/R43) and an **MX1.25 speaker header** driven by an **NS4150B** amp whose enable is `PA_CTRL` = **expander EXIO7**; a **6 Ω 1 W speaker ships in the box**. Codec control (`AU_SCL`/`AU_SDA`) is on the existing IO7/IO8 I²C bus. Because the I²S bus is private (IO12–16), **audio and the stepper cannot physically conflict** — this is the only viable voice-input path, and it needs no new parts and no motor changes. ⚠️ Firmware must not drive 12/13/15/16 as GPIOs once the codec is enabled. NuttX side: `nuttx/drivers/audio/es8311.c` supports `AUDIO_TYPE_INPUT`, and `esp32s3_i2s.c` has `i2s_receive()` with `CONFIG_ESP32S3_I2S0_RX` default y. No ASR engine exists in the tree — keyword spotting would be TFLM, or cloud via `external/bailian_sdk`.
87	
88	## Features this board unlocks (deferred in emulator)
89	- **RTC (PCF85063)** → real **meal-timing** (was skipped for lack of a wall clock).
90	- **microSD** → **persistent feed history / analytics** across reboots (was in-memory only).
91	
92	## Feeder dispensing — grams -> motion (calibration)
93	The app speaks **grams** (portions ~5-50g, daily limits 20-300g; NOT kg). The dispenser does not measure grams; it is CALIBRATED once:
94	- Measure kibble released per unit of motion: run the auger 1 rotation (or motor 1 s), weigh the output on a kitchen scale -> e.g. `grams_per_rotation` ~= 5g (or `grams_per_second` ~= 8g). Store the constant (NVS/SD so it survives reboot).
95	- **Dispense N grams = run actuator for N / grams_per_unit** (e.g. 20g @ 5g/rot = 4 rotations, or 2.5s @ 8g/s).
96	- This is OPEN-LOOP feeding (no sensor): ~±10-20% accurate, standard for consumer feeders. Fine for v1.
97	
98	**Firmware hook:** `velapaw_feeder_dispense(grams)` (currently mock print) becomes on hardware: `runtime = grams / grams_per_second; drive_servo(GPIO43 LEDC PWM, runtime);`. Nothing above it changes (app stays in grams). Planned backend: hal/feeder_servo.c.
99	
100	**Accuracy upgrade (deferred):** add a **load cell + HX711** under the bowl -> CLOSED-LOOP: dispense until measured weight == target (~1g accurate). Same hardware also gives real EATEN-grams / eating-speed (the analytics we deferred). Needs the load cell (not on the board).
101	
102	**Suggested (not yet built):** a UI "Calibrate" mode = dispense a test amount -> user weighs it -> enter value -> stores grams_per_unit.

11	The VelaPaw feeder's **28BYJ-48 + ULN2003 finally rotates** (2026-07-23). Coils: IN1=GPIO9, IN2=GPIO10, IN3=GPIO11, **IN4=GPIO43** (was 44).
12	
13	**Root cause of the long "vibrates but shaft won't turn" saga:** IN4 on **GPIO44 (U0RXD)** stayed clamped high even after re-asserting `esp32s3_configgpio(pin, OUTPUT)` before every dispense — the UART0 re-mux wins over the GPIO reclaim on that pin. Moving IN4 to **GPIO43 (U0TXD)** fixed it instantly; shaft turns on the first feed.
14	
15	**Second root cause, found 2026-08-02 from the schematic netlist:** the pre-bring-up code had IN1/IN2/IN3 on **GPIO12/13/15**, which are the ES8311 codec's I²S lines and are **not routed to the J8 header at all** (each net has exactly two nodes: ESP32 + codec). So for part of the saga three of the four coils were electrically unconnected — no coil-order table could ever have worked. Moving them to 9/10/11 (the unused microSD pins, the board's only reusable native GPIOs) is what made all four coils real. See [[velapaw-hardware]] for the full J8 map.
16	
17	**Why:** we burned many build/flash cycles chasing coil-order tables. Don't. The straight full-step table `{0x3,0x6,0xC,0x9}` (bit0=IN1..bit3=IN4) is the correct textbook 28BYJ-48 sequence. All 3 distinct coil-order topologies were swept and NONE turned — because the fault was one dead pin (44), not the sequence. A confident external "fix" to `{0x5,0x6,0xA,0x9}` was just re-proposing a sweep candidate we'd already tested.
18	
19	**How to apply:** keep IN4 on GPIO43. `feeder_pins_output()` (configgpio OUTPUT on all four) is still called at the start of `board_feeder_dispense` — harmless, keep it. STEP_PER_REV 2048 full-step, STEP_DELAY_US 3000 (~333 steps/s, within pull-in torque), one-direction ratchet.
20	
21	**Repo reconciled 2026-08-02.** The Windows repo copy of `board/esp32s3_st7789.c` had drifted badly from the VM: it carried a half-step table `k_halfstep[8]` (`STEP_PER_REV 4096`, `STEP_DELAY_US 1500`, `GRAMS_PER_POCKET 4`) with **bit3=IN1** — the *opposite* bit order to what runs. A rebuild from Windows would have turned the rotor backwards. Now matches the VM: full-step, `{0x3,0x6,0xC,0x9}`, bit0=IN1, 2048/3000µs/5g, plus `feeder_pins_output()` re-called at the top of `board_feeder_dispense`. See [[velapaw-golden-baseline]].
22	
23	**Still TODO:** (1) confirm rotation direction actually carries food inlet→outlet (reverse the phase index if backward); (2) calibrate `GRAMS_PER_POCKET` — currently placeholder 5, weigh one pocket; (3) add a fractional-step accumulator: 2048/6 = 341, and 341×6 = 2046, so straight integer pockets lose 2 steps/rev and the vane drifts over hundreds of dispenses.
24

Yes, it will work, and the firmware doesn't need to change. Your motor is the 5 V version, though (the sticker on it should say 5VDC), so 9 V runs it above its rating. In this feeder that's acceptable, with a few precautions.

**What 9 V does**
- **Current and heat:** the coils draw roughly twice the current, about 0.3 A instead of 0.15 A, and get 3–4 times hotter while the motor turns. You also get more torque.
- **Why that's acceptable:** a meal only turns the motor for about 3 seconds, and the board code switches all four coils off after every turn ([esp32s3_st7789.c:485](D:/openVela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge/board/esp32s3_st7789.c#L485)). So the heat never builds up, and the battery draws almost nothing between meals. Avoid long back-to-back test spins, and stop if the motor gets too hot to touch.
- **Driver board:** the ULN2003 board takes 5–12 V, so it's fine.
- **Battery life:** each meal uses about 0.25 mAh, so even this battery should last well over a hundred meals. The 6F22 in the listing is the cheapest (carbon-zinc) kind. An alkaline 9 V, marked 6LR61, holds about twice as much and its voltage drops less under load.

**Before you plug it in**
1. **Check polarity with your meter.** The plug's centre pin should read +9 V against the outer sleeve. Your adapter is centre-positive too (that's the symbol on its label), so they should match. The driver board has no protection if the polarity is reversed.
2. **Keep the 9 V away from the ESP32 board.**
   - The battery's + goes to the driver board only.
   - Never connect it to J8 pin 1 (VBAT), J8 pin 2 (VBUS) or the board's USB-C. 9 V there would destroy the board.
   - GND is the only connection the two should share. Keep the GND wire between the driver board and J8, or the motor won't step.
3. **Check the plug fits your socket.** The battery lead is 5.5 × 2.1 mm.
4. **Test before the finals.** Run a few test feeds, and bring the 5 V adapter and a spare battery as backups.

**If you just want to get rid of the wall plug**
- There's an option that keeps the motor at its rated 5 V: a USB-to-DC barrel cable from a spare USB port on the laptop.
  - Get a plain 5 V cable, not a 9 V/12 V "boost" cable.
- Don't use a power bank. Most switch themselves off after about 30 seconds of near-zero draw, and that's exactly what the motor draws between meals.

## 1. Primary Request and Intent

**Current request (just received, not yet answered).** The user sent two photos:
- **Their present motor supply:** an AC/DC adaptor labelled MODEL 0520, INPUT AC100-240V 50/60Hz, OUTPUT 5V⎓2A, with a centre-positive polarity symbol.
- **What they want to buy:** a Pinduoduo listing for a TIANQIU 6F22 9V battery with a snap lead to a DC barrel plug, sold as "aeduino UNO R3 Power Supply, 9V Battery 6F22…", ¥2.3 discounted or ¥7 bought alone.

They asked: "Currently the stepmotor is using the 5v 2a but i want to replace it with the 9v is it possiblr". They want to know whether the feeder's stepper can run from the 9V battery instead of the 5V 2A wall adapter.

**Completed earlier in this session:**
- **Feeding times checked.** The "next meal at 08:23" is the 20-minute gap after the last meal eaten, not a fault. The 07:55 meal was eaten at 08:03, so the 08:10 meal is held until 08:23. Advice: set the second morning meal to 08:25 or later.
- **"write the chinese version of the slides": DONE.** It is a separate, fully Chinese finals deck. The English deck was not touched. The reply has been sent and memory updated.

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

### Stepper hardware
- **Motor:** 28BYJ-48, the **5 V version, confirmed** in July. The 12V listing video was marketing.
- **Driver:** a ULN2003 board. Its supply input accepts 5–12 V, and the ULN2003A chip is rated to 50 V and 500 mA per channel.
- **Coil current:**
  - The coils are about 50 Ω per phase.
  - At 5 V, after the ULN2003's ~1 V drop, that is about 80 mA per phase, or roughly 0.16–0.24 A with two coils on.
  - At 9 V it is about 160 mA per phase, or about 0.32 A with two on.
  - Heat per coil rises about 3–4× (1.28 W vs 0.34 W).
- **Power wiring:**
  - The motor and ULN2003 run from a **separate 5 V ≥2 A supply, sharing ground only** with the board.
  - The board is powered over USB-C from the laptop.
  - Coil lines IN1–IN4 = GPIO 9/10/11/43, on J8 pins 14/12/10/27.
  - J8 power pins: pin 1 VBAT, pin 2 **VBUS**, pins 3/4/29/30 GND, pins 31/32 3V3.

### Stepper firmware
- Full-step table `{0x3,0x6,0xC,0x9}`: two coils are energised at every step.
- STEP_PER_REV is 2048; STEP_PER_POCKET is about 341; STEP_DELAY_US is 3000 µs, about 333 steps/s.
- **The coils are de-energised at rest:** `step_coils(0)` runs at init and after every dispense.
- A meal is about 3 pockets, roughly 3 s of running.

### The 9 V battery
- 6F22 is the zinc-carbon designation; the alkaline equivalent is 6LR61.
- Capacity is small: a few hundred mAh at light load, much less at 0.3 A.

## 5. Problem Solving
- The feeding-times question and the Chinese deck are both done.
- **9V question: research is done; the answer is ready but not sent.** Plan for the answer:
  - **Short answer:** yes, it will run. The ULN2003 board takes 5–12 V, and no firmware change is needed. But it isn't the best swap.
  - **Over-voltage:** the motor is the 5 V 28BYJ-48. At 9 V the current roughly doubles (~0.3 A vs ~0.2 A) and the coils run about 3–4× hotter. That is out of spec, but survivable here only because the firmware switches all coils off after each dispense, so each meal is only about 3 s of running.
  - **Physical check:** after a feed, all four ULN2003 LEDs must be off. If any stays lit, don't use 9 V.
  - **The battery is the weak point:**
    - A 6F22 is carbon-zinc with a small capacity, and its voltage sags at 0.3 A.
    - It could manage many meals, since the coils are off when idle, but there's no charge indicator, and a flat battery mid-demo means no food. Carry a spare if they go this way.
  - **Safety if they use it:**
    - Only GND is shared with the board. The battery + goes only to the ULN2003's + pin, never to J8 VBUS (pin 2), 3V3 or VBAT.
    - Check the plug fits the jack (5.5×2.1 vs 5.5×2.5) and is centre-positive, like the adapter's label.
    - Feel the motor after a few feeds: warm is fine, too hot to hold is not.
  - **Better option:**
    - A USB-to-5.5×2.1 DC cable from a power bank, the laptop's spare USB port or a phone charger: 5 V, in spec, and ~0.2 A is fine for any USB port.
    - Or a 5 V buck module (or a 7805) between the 9 V battery and the driver.
    - Do NOT power the motor from the board's VBUS pin: the motor's current pulses could brown out the board during recognition.
  - **Ask their goal:** fewer wall plugs, or more torque? If torque, a slower STEP_DELAY_US is the in-spec fix, but that needs new firmware, which is only built after a yes.

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

### Stepper hardware
- **Motor:** 28BYJ-48, the **5 V version, confirmed** in July. The 12V listing video was marketing.
- **Driver:** a ULN2003 board. Its supply input accepts 5–12 V, and the ULN2003A chip is rated to 50 V and 500 mA per channel.
- **Coil current:**
  - The coils are about 50 Ω per phase.
  - At 5 V, after the ULN2003's ~1 V drop, that is about 80 mA per phase, or roughly 0.16–0.24 A with two coils on.
  - At 9 V it is about 160 mA per phase, or about 0.32 A with two on.
  - Heat per coil rises about 3–4× (1.28 W vs 0.34 W).
- **Power wiring:**
  - The motor and ULN2003 run from a **separate 5 V ≥2 A supply, sharing ground only** with the board.
  - The board is powered over USB-C from the laptop.
  - Coil lines IN1–IN4 = GPIO 9/10/11/43, on J8 pins 14/12/10/27.
  - J8 power pins: pin 1 VBAT, pin 2 **VBUS**, pins 3/4/29/30 GND, pins 31/32 3V3.

### Stepper firmware
- Full-step table `{0x3,0x6,0xC,0x9}`: two coils are energised at every step.
- STEP_PER_REV is 2048; STEP_PER_POCKET is about 341; STEP_DELAY_US is 3000 µs, about 333 steps/s.
- **The coils are de-energised at rest:** `step_coils(0)` runs at init and after every dispense.
- A meal is about 3 pockets, roughly 3 s of running.

### The 9 V battery
- 6F22 is the zinc-carbon designation; the alkaline equivalent is 6LR61.
- Capacity is small: a few hundred mAh at light load, much less at 0.3 A.
- Internal resistance is high, so the voltage sags under load, and there's no way to see how much charge is left.

## 5. Problem Solving
- The feeding-times question and the Chinese deck are both done.
- **9V question: research is done; the answer is ready but not sent.** Plan for the answer:
  - **Short answer:** yes, it will run. The ULN2003 board takes 5–12 V, and no firmware change is needed. But it isn't the best swap.
  - **Over-voltage:** the motor is the 5 V 28BYJ-48. At 9 V the current roughly doubles (~0.3 A vs ~0.2 A) and the coils run about 3–4× hotter. That is out of spec, but survivable here only because the firmware switches all coils off after each dispense, so each meal is only about 3 s of running.
  - **Physical check:** after a feed, all four ULN2003 LEDs must be off. If any stays lit, don't use 9 V.
  - **The battery is the weak point:**
    - A 6F22 is carbon-zinc with a small capacity, and its voltage sags at 0.3 A.
    - It could manage many meals, since the coils are off when idle, but there's no charge indicator, and a flat battery mid-demo means no food. Carry a spare if they go this way.
  - **Safety if they use it:**
    - Only GND is shared with the board. The battery + goes only to the ULN2003's + pin, never to J8 VBUS (pin 2), 3V3 or VBAT.
    - Check the plug fits the jack (5.5×2.1 vs 5.5×2.5) and is centre-positive, like the adapter's label.
    - Feel the motor after a few feeds: warm is fine, too hot to hold is not.
  - **Better option:**
    - A USB-to-5.5×2.1 DC cable from a power bank, the laptop's spare USB port or a phone charger: 5 V, in spec, and ~0.2 A is fine for any USB port.
    - Or a 5 V buck module (or a 7805) between the 9 V battery and the driver.
    - Do NOT power the motor from the board's VBUS pin: the motor's current pulses could brown out the board during recognition.
  - **Ask their goal:** fewer wall plugs, or more torque? If torque, a slower STEP_DELAY_US is the in-spec fix, but that needs new firmware, which is only built after a yes.

Yes, it will work, and the firmware doesn't need to change. Your motor is the 5 V version, though (the sticker on it should say 5VDC), so 9 V runs it above its rating. In this feeder that's acceptable, with a few precautions.

**What 9 V does**
- **Current and heat:** the coils draw roughly twice the current, about 0.3 A instead of 0.15 A, and get 3–4 times hotter while the motor turns. You also get more torque.
- **Why that's acceptable:** a meal only turns the motor for about 3 seconds, and the board code switches all four coils off after every turn ([esp32s3_st7789.c:485](D:/openVela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge/board/esp32s3_st7789.c#L485)). So the heat never builds up, and the battery draws almost nothing between meals. Avoid long back-to-back test spins, and stop if the motor gets too hot to touch.
- **Driver board:** the ULN2003 board takes 5–12 V, so it's fine.
- **Battery life:** each meal uses about 0.25 mAh, so even this battery should last well over a hundred meals. The 6F22 in the listing is the cheapest (carbon-zinc) kind. An alkaline 9 V, marked 6LR61, holds about twice as much and its voltage drops less under load.

**Before you plug it in**
1. **Check polarity with your meter.** The plug's centre pin should read +9 V against the outer sleeve. Your adapter is centre-positive too (that's the symbol on its label), so they should match. The driver board has no protection if the polarity is reversed.
2. **Keep the 9 V away from the ESP32 board.**
   - The battery's + goes to the driver board only.
   - Never connect it to J8 pin 1 (VBAT), J8 pin 2 (VBUS) or the board's USB-C. 9 V there would destroy the board.
   - GND is the only connection the two should share. Keep the GND wire between the driver board and J8, or the motor won't step.
3. **Check the plug fits your socket.** The battery lead is 5.5 × 2.1 mm.
4. **Test before the finals.** Run a few test feeds, and bring the 5 V adapter and a spare battery as backups.

**If you just want to get rid of the wall plug**
- There's an option that keeps the motor at its rated 5 V: a USB-to-DC barrel cable from a spare USB port on the laptop.
  - Get a plain 5 V cable, not a 9 V/12 V "boost" cable.
- Don't use a power bank. Most switch themselves off after about 30 seconds of near-zero draw, and that's exactly what the motor draws between meals.

Abstract

93 94

An ordinary timed feeder cannot tell which animal is standing at the bowl, so in a multi-pet household per-pet portioning and per-pet weight control are impossible — and per-pet portioning is the first thing a vet prescribes. VelaPaw, built on openVela (NuttX) and a Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C, identifies the individual pet on-device from a single camera and gates dispensing on two conditions together: the pet is recognised, and one of its meals is due today and unfed. Recognition uses open-set metric learning rather than classification — the model emits only a 128-dimensional L2-normalised embedding, so enrolling a new pet is a pure runtime operation requiring no retraining and no firmware update. Measured results: porting an INT8 operator library to Xtensa LX7, for which openVela ships none, cut inference from 6.75 s to 1.31 s; tracing a display fault with a logic analyser to panel bit-desynchronisation allowed a move to 40 MHz hardware SPI with GDMA, cutting full-screen repaint from 246 ms to 61 ms; and trimming 20 unused tools compressed the ai_agent request body from 19,391 B to fit NuttX's IOB pool, taking end-to-end latency from 150–300 s to 3.6–35.6 s. All image processing and every feeding decision happen on-device and no image ever leaves the hardware; the only networked component, ai_agent, uses a custom Skill to read the records the feeder writes to littlefs and speaks only when an appetite threshold is crossed. Unplugged from the network, the feeder behaves identically.

3. Technical Report

97 98

3.1 Introduction

99 100

3.1.1 Background and problem statement

101 102

In a multi-pet household, an ordinary timed feeder has a structural flaw: it does not know which animal is standing at the bowl. The lid opens on schedule, whoever arrives first eats everything, and the slower one goes hungry. Per-pet portions, per-pet weight control, per-pet appetite monitoring — none of it is possible. And per-pet portioning is precisely the first thing a vet asks for when prescribing a weight-loss, disease-management, or post-operative plan.

103 104

Existing camera-equipped feeders — for instance the Xiaomi Mijia Smart Pet Feeder 2 Vision Edition, launched March 2026 at ¥449 crowdfunded / ¥549 retail — solve the problem of letting the owner see the bowl; what the camera produces is a video stream. They do not solve identifying which animal it is. Such products also bind the camera feed to a cloud account, which is the single largest source of hesitation pet owners have about a household camera.

105 106

VelaPaw therefore defines its problem as:

107
108 On an MCU-class device, with no network, no cloud, and no phone app, use a single camera to tell which pet is at the bowl, and dispense only the meal that pet is due right now; then keep a long-term record of each pet's intake and proactively tell the owner when appetite goes wrong. 109
110 111

That last "proactively tell the owner" layer is carried by openVela's ai_agent framework and is the only part of the system that needs a network. The feeder itself behaves identically offline.

112 113

3.1.2 Technical challenges

114 115 116 117 118 119 120 121 122 123 124 125 126 127 128 129
ChallengeWhat it looked like
① Compute for fine-grained on-device recognitionIndividual pet ID is a fine-grained recognition problem requiring a MobileNet-class backbone plus a metric-learning head. Running that model on Xtensa LX7 through TFLite-Micro's reference kernels takes ≈6.75 s per inference — unusable. An early TFLM spike (docs/TFLM_SPIKE_REPORT.md, run in QEMU, not on S3) profiled a comparable INT8 CNN and found CONV_2D accounts for 84% of the clock (643,819 of 768,105 ticks): latency is almost entirely decided by the INT8 convolution kernels. Yet the openVela tree ships only cmsis-nn (ARM) and nnlib-hifi4 (HiFi DSP) — there is no operator library for LX7.
② Adding a pet must not require retrainingNo consumer product can ask a user to retrain a model to add a cat. N-way classification had to be abandoned in favour of open-set metric learning, with a threshold that holds up under real household lighting.
③ The model does not fit the MCU's memory mapA 1.44 MB identity model cannot be memory-mapped as a const array — the ESP32-S3 DROM0 MMU window saturates well before that. It must be read from raw flash into PSRAM; but a flash read suspends the CPU cache, and PSRAM is reached through that cache, so if the loading thread's stack lives in PSRAM the whole SoC deadlocks.
④ The hardware-SPI display "renders nothing"Full-screen writes worked; any partial window (a CASET/RASET sub-rectangle followed by RAMWR) never appeared — while the identical byte sequence over bit-banged GPIO worked perfectly. This survived roughly 60 rounds of blind rebuilds.
⑤ ai_agent's request body vs. the network bufferai_agent registers 36 tools by default, whose JSON schemas push a single LLM request body to 19,391 B, of which 9,946 B is tool schema. NuttX's IOB pool is only NBUFFERS(64) × BUFSIZE(196) = 12,544 B, leaving roughly 7,840 B usable after THROTTLE(24). The request is far larger than the available buffer; the symptom is an intermittent hang with no timeout.
⑥ Agent answers that look right but are fabricatedThe heartbeat replayed its own history; list_dir's prefix match plus a local-tool shortcut handed (no files found) straight to the user as a final answer; ask was truncated at the seventh word by MAX_ARGS. None of these raise an error — they simply make the answer fluent and wrong.
130 131

3.1.3 Innovations

132 133
    134
  1. Dual-condition "recognition × schedule" gating. Food is dispensed only when "this is that pet" and "one of its meals is due today and has not been fed" are both true — at most once per meal per day, with any meal individually skippable. Recognition alone would feed the greedy one all day; a timer alone would feed whoever happened to walk past. This AND gate is the core product logic and the precondition for per-pet portioning to mean anything.
    2. 135
  2. Open-set metric learning instead of a classifier. The model is only a generic pet feature extractor, mapping a 128×128 frame to an L2-normalised 128-dimensional embedding. Enrolment = store the mean embedding of a few photos; recognition = cosine similarity. Adding a pet is a pure runtime operation — no retraining, no firmware update.
    3. 136
  3. A bug that survived 60 rebuilds turned into a 4× speedup. A logic analyser disproved the "software problem" hypothesis and reframed it as a panel bit-synchronisation problem (§3.4.3). With that fixed, the display moved from bit-banging to 40 MHz hardware SPI + GDMA: full-screen repaint 246 ms → 61 ms.
    4. 137
  4. ai_agent as a silent health monitor, not a chatbot. A heartbeat task periodically reads the records the feeder itself wrote to flash and speaks only when a threshold is crossed. When everything is fine, the device says nothing. The custom Skill states explicitly that only numbers from those files may be used, and nothing may be invented.
    5. 138
  5. A clear "offline-first, network-optional" boundary. Every feeding decision and all image processing happen on-device; no image ever leaves the device. Unplug the network and the feeder behaves identically — only the Agent layer stops. This is both a privacy claim and a reliability claim.
    6. 139
  6. Pocket-by-pocket mechanical dosing. A continuously rotating paddle rotor replaces a flap: a flap's dose drifts with hopper level, whereas each rotor pocket has fixed volume, so grams = pockets × grams-per-pocket — making per-pet portioning true at the mechanical level too.

An honest reading of this result: EER 0.291 is a lower-bound-style figure measured on 39 individuals from a public pet dataset under open-set conditions. 3.7.2 Market outlook and commercial value

661 662

Market signal. In March 2026 Xiaomi launched the Mijia Smart Pet Feeder 2 Vision Edition (¥449 crowdfunded / ¥549 retail) — a mass-market product built specifically to bring a camera into the feeding scenario. That is the company with the best read on what pet owners will pay for, independently validating VelaPaw's founding judgement with real money: the camera belongs on the feeder. VelaPaw takes the same judgement one step further — from "see the bowl" to "know which one it is", entirely on-device.

663 664

Target users, in order of willingness to pay:

665
    666
  1. Multi-pet households (core). The sharpest pain: portion management simply does not work with more than one animal. This is the one group whose problem cannot be solved without individual recognition.
    2. 667
  2. Owners managing prescription diets or weight loss. A vet's gram-level plan has to actually be executed and recorded; VelaPaw's daily caps plus per-pet history are exactly that record of execution.
    3. 668
  3. Privacy-sensitive owners. People unwilling to have household camera footage enter any cloud account. "Images never leave the device" is a hard property here, not a privacy-policy clause.
    4. 669
  4. Carers of senior pets. A drop in appetite is the earliest signal of many illnesses; proactive push turns "the owner must log this daily" into "the device speaks up when something is wrong".
    5. 670
671 672

Business model. The core is one-time hardware sales with no subscription — a structural advantage that comes directly from on-device AI: with no cloud inference cost, there is no cost to amortise through a subscription.
